title: Essential Redis Commands
description: Learn the most commonly used Redis commands across data types, including atomic counters, bulk operations, and expiration patterns.

data.text: Redis exposes a flat command space where every operation is atomic and runs in constant or logarithmic time. Mastering a small set of commands is enough to build production caching, rate limiting, and job queues.

rows: Push left, pop right for queues

data.text: Atomic counters remove the need for application-level locking. Redis guarantees that `INCR` is safe even when many clients call it at the same time. Use this pattern for rate limiters, view counts, and inventory decrements.

data.title: Avoid KEYS * in production
data.text: The KEYS command blocks Redis while scanning every key. Always use SCAN for production key iteration. KEYS is safe only in development or emergency debugging.

data.title: Common expiration strategies
items: **TTL on set** — set EX or PX flags when writing the value.
**Late binding** — set expiration only on the first increment so counters never expire before use.
**Group expiry** — add a shared timestamp field to a Hash so related fields expire together.

data.caption: Command selection by access pattern
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Single value?] -->|Yes| B[GET / SET]
    A -->|No| C[Object fields?]
    C -->|Yes| D[HGET / HSET]
    C -->|No| E[Ordered queue?]
    E -->|Yes| F[LPUSH / RPOP]
    E -->|No| G[Unique collection?]
    G -->|Scored| H[ZADD / ZRANGE]
    G -->|Unscored| I[SADD / SMEMBERS]

items.question: Are Redis commands really atomic?
items.answer: Yes. Every single Redis command executes atomically. For multiple commands, use transactions (MULTI/EXEC) or Lua scripts when you need atomicity across more than one operation.

items.question: When should I use a Lua script?
items.answer: Use Lua scripts when you need read-modify-write semantics that span multiple keys or data types. Lua runs atomically on the Redis server.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Master GET, SET, INCR, EXPIRE, DEL, SCAN, and the type-specific CRUD commands first.
Use pipelines to batch commands and reduce network latency.
Prefer SCAN over KEYS for any production key lookup.
